conversation.content:
Hi there—my name is Maya, and I’m a clinician who specializes in helping new moms navigate the emotional ups and downs that can come after childbirth. I’ll be guiding you through a short questionnaire called the EPDS, which screens for depressive and anxiety symptoms and includes a question about self-harm. It’s simply a way to check in on how you’ve been feeling over the past seven days so we can make sure you’re getting the support you deserve.

Everything you share today is confidential, and this is a judgment-free space. We’ll go through ten questions; I’ll ask each one conversationally, and you can answer in your own words—no need to worry about choosing from a list. When you’re ready, we can begin.

First question: Over the past week, have you been able to laugh and see the funny side of things, or has that felt difficult?

Honestly, I used to laugh all the time—my husband and I would joke about everything—but lately it feels like I’m faking it. I’ll smile when someone shows me a cute baby video, but the laughter feels kind of hollow, like I’m doing it because I’m supposed to, not because it feels good.
I have been able to laugh and see the funny side of things

Most of the time, no. A couple of nights ago my husband tried to cheer me up with a silly meme he knows I normally love, and I just… couldn’t. I pretended to laugh so he wouldn’t worry, but nothing felt funny.
I have looked forward with enjoyment to things

Not really. I used to get excited about little stuff—coffee with a friend, a new episode of my show—but now even planning those things feels like one more chore. I still go through the motions, but the happy “can’t-wait” feeling is pretty much gone.
I have blamed myself unnecessarily when things went wrong

Yeah… I do that a lot. Yesterday the baby wouldn’t settle for his nap and I kept thinking it must be something I’m doing wrong—maybe I’m not swaddling tight enough or I missed his sleepy window. My head knows babies just cry, but I still feel like I’m failing him every time it happens.
I have been anxious or worried for no good reason

Pretty much all day, every day. I’ll be feeding him and suddenly my heart races because I’m sure he’s not breathing right, or I’ll lie awake picturing him rolling off the changing table even when I’m right there. I know it’s “for no good reason,” but I can’t shut the thoughts off.
I have felt scared or panicky for no very good reason

Yeah, that’s been happening. Sometimes out of nowhere my chest gets tight, my hands feel shaky, and I’m convinced something awful is about to happen—like the house is unsafe or I’ll drop him. It passes after a few minutes, but it leaves me rattled.
Things have been getting on top of me

Most days, honestly. There are moments when the pile of laundry, the dishes, the feedings, the constant checking on him—it all feels like it’s crushing me. I’ll stand in the middle of the living room and just stare because I don’t know which thing to do first, and then I feel like I’m drowning. I keep telling myself to push through, but it’s hard.
I have been so unhappy that I have had difficulty sleeping

Yes. I lie down exhausted, but my brain keeps circling—did I sterilize the bottles right, is he breathing, am I doing any of this motherhood thing right? I’ll finally drift off around two, then pop awake at the tiniest grunt from the bassinet. By morning I feel like I’ve barely slept, even when the baby actually stayed down.
I have felt sad or miserable

That’s how I feel most of the day. I wake up with this heavy, gray mood that just sticks around. I’ll look at the baby and feel love, but it’s like there’s a thick blanket over everything—no energy, no real joy, just this constant ache in my chest that won’t go away.
I have been so unhappy that I have been crying

Yeah, a few times this week. Two nights ago I just sat in the rocker after finally getting him down, and the tears started coming—I couldn’t even name why. It’s like the sadness just builds up until it leaks out.
The thought of harming myself has occurred to me
No, I haven’t had any thoughts like that. I feel low, but I’ve never thought about hurting myself. I just want to feel better so I can be the mom my baby needs.

You've shared how the joy you once found in everyday moments feels distant now, replaced by a persistent heaviness and worry that shadows each day. The laughter that used to come easily with your husband has become hollow, and planning simple pleasures feels like one more chore. You describe feeling crushed by ordinary tasks, lying awake with racing thoughts about your baby's safety, and experiencing sudden surges of panic even when you know there's no real danger. Despite these overwhelming feelings, you remain committed to caring for your son and have not had thoughts of harming yourself, and you want more than anything to feel like yourself again so you can be the mother you know he deserves.
**Screening Impression:** Total EPDS Score: 25, Risk Level: Probable depression, urgent referral (concerns include <sym>Patient explicitly states "Most of the time, no" and describes being unable to laugh even at a meme she normally loves, aligning with "Not at all."</sym>, <sym>Patient reports a marked reduction in anticipatory enjoyment, aligning with "Definitely less than I ever did"</sym>, <sym>Patient reports frequent, persistent self-blame ('I do that a lot') with specific examples, matching 'Yes, most of the time</sym>, <sym>Patient reports anxiety "pretty much all day, every day" with intrusive catastrophic thoughts that are pervasive and uncontrollable, matching "Yes, very often."</sym>, <sym>Patient describes sudden, intense physical panic with catastrophic fears, matching the "Yes, quite a lot" option.</sym>, <sym>Patient says "Most days" and describes feeling crushed, drowning, and unable to decide what to do, matching "most of the time I haven't been able to cope at all"</sym>, <sym>Patient describes nightly insomnia driven by distressing, racing thoughts and hypervigilance, consistent with 'most of the time</sym>, <sym>Patient describes persistent, pervasive low mood "most of the day" with physical heaviness and absence of joy, aligning with "Yes, most of the time"</sym>, <sym>Patient describes multiple crying episodes this week with unprovoked, overwhelming sadness—semantically aligns with "Yes, quite often."</sym>)
**Reasoning:** Your EPDS score of 25 clearly exceeds the clinical cut-off of 14 that flags probable <med>major depressive disorder with peripartum onset</med>. The pattern of high scores across mood, cognitive, anxiety, and somatic items aligns with DSM-5 criteria: depressed mood most of the day, markedly diminished interest or pleasure, feelings of worthlessness, excessive guilt, recurrent panic, and insomnia. The severity and daily frequency of <sym>anxiety</sym> and <sym>panic symptoms</sym> also suggest co-occurring <med>peripartum anxiety</med>. Denial of self-harm thoughts is a protective factor but does not lessen the urgency for comprehensive assessment and treatment. This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.
**Recommended Next Steps/Support Options:**
1. Arrange urgent appointment with your <med>primary care provider</med> or <med>perinatal mental health specialist</med> within the next few days
2. Ask about evidence-based treatments such as <med>CBT</med> or <med>IPT</med> and discuss risks and benefits of <med>antidepressant medication</med> compatible with breastfeeding
3. Involve a trusted adult to help with overnight infant care so you can implement basic sleep-hygiene practices
4. Schedule follow-up EPDS in two weeks to monitor progress and safety
5. Keep national perinatal mental health helpline numbers accessible for after-hours support
Disclaimer: This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.

postpartum depression screening impression for patient with EPDS score 25: Postpartum Depression / Anxiety Screening Note – [today’s date]

**Identified symptoms / behavioral concerns**
- Persistent low mood, described as “heavy, gray,” present most of the day
- Marked anhedonia: minimal ability to laugh or anticipate enjoyment
- Daily excessive guilt/self-blame regarding infant care
- Near-constant, intrusive worry and panic symptoms (racing heart, shakiness, fears of infant harm)
- Frequent crying spells without clear trigger
- Sleep disturbance secondary to ruminative worry, not simply infant demands
- Overwhelm/“drowning” sensation interfering with basic task initiation

**Consistency across items**
All mood, cognitive, and somatic responses cluster toward the severe end; no reported period of euthymia since delivery. Anxiety symptoms appear equally prominent.

**Screening significance / risk flags**
- Meets clinical cut-off for probable major depressive episode with peripartum onset
- Co-occurring anxiety/panic features
- NO current self-harm ideation (item 10 denied) → documented as protective factor

**Plan / next steps (screening only)**
Recommend expedited referral for comprehensive psychiatric evaluation and follow-up support services. Continue routine safety monitoring.
